title: The Brainstem
summary: Midbrain, pons and medulla: tiny, crowded and vital.

lessons.title: Brainstem Overview & Landmarks

levels.kid:
Your brainstem is like a thick stalk that holds up your brain, the way a stem holds up a flower. It connects your brain to your spinal cord.

It has three parts, stacked from top to bottom: the midbrain, the pons and the medulla.

The brainstem is small, about as long as your thumb, but it does huge jobs. It keeps you breathing and keeps your heart beating, even while you sleep. It also helps you wake up.

Lots of special nerves come out of it, like wires. They let you move your eyes, chew, smile, hear and swallow.

Every message going between your brain and your body passes through this busy little stalk.
levels.hs:
The **brainstem** connects the cerebrum above to the spinal cord below. It sits in the back of the skull (the **posterior fossa**) in front of the cerebellum. From top to bottom it has three parts:

- **Midbrain** (mesencephalon): the shortest part, just below the thalamus
- **Pons**: the bulging middle part, Latin for "bridge"
- **Medulla oblongata**: the lowest part, which becomes the spinal cord at the foramen magnum

The brainstem does three big jobs. First, it is a **highway**: every motor command going down and every sensation going up passes through it. Second, it holds the nuclei of **cranial nerves III to XII**, which control the eyes, face, mouth, throat and neck. Third, it contains centers for **breathing, heart rate, blood pressure and wakefulness**.

A useful rule of four: cranial nerves III and IV come from the midbrain, V to VIII from the pons, and IX to XII from the medulla.

On the front you can see the **cerebral peduncles**, the bulging pons and the **pyramids** of the medulla. On the back are four bumps called the **colliculi** and the floor of the **fourth ventricle**.

Because so much is packed into so little space, even a tiny stroke in the brainstem can cause major problems, and a large one can be fatal.
levels.college:
**Gross divisions and zones.** The brainstem runs from the diencephalon to the spinal cord at the foramen magnum (just above the C1 rootlets). Each level has three longitudinal zones: the dorsal **tectum** (only in the midbrain: superior and inferior colliculi), the central **tegmentum** (cranial nerve nuclei, reticular formation, ascending tracts) and the ventral **basis** (crus cerebri, basilar pons, pyramids), which carries descending corticofugal fibers.

**Ventral landmarks.** Cerebral peduncles flank the **interpeduncular fossa**, where CN III exits. The basilar pons carries the **basilar sulcus** for the basilar artery; CN V emerges laterally from it. At the pontomedullary junction CN VI exits medially and CN VII and VIII exit laterally at the **cerebellopontine angle**. On the medulla, CN XII exits in the **preolivary sulcus** (between pyramid and olive); CN IX, X and XI exit in the **postolivary sulcus**. The pyramidal decussation marks the lower end of the medulla.

**Dorsal landmarks.** CN IV is the only nerve to exit dorsally, just below the inferior colliculus. The rhomboid floor of the fourth ventricle shows the **facial colliculus** (abducens nucleus plus the internal genu of CN VII), the hypoglossal and vagal trigones, the **area postrema** and the **obex**. The gracile and cuneate tubercles sit below.

**Cerebellar peduncles.** Superior (mainly output, to midbrain), middle (input from pontine nuclei) and inferior (input from spinal cord and medulla).

**Organization rule.** Motor nuclei lie medial and sensory nuclei lateral, separated by the **sulcus limitans**. The **rule of four** adds that the medial structures are motor tracts, medial lemniscus, MLF and the motor nuclei of III, IV, VI and XII; lateral structures are the spinothalamic and spinocerebellar tracts, the sensory nucleus of V and descending sympathetic fibers.

**Blood supply.** Vertebrobasilar: paramedian, short circumferential and long circumferential branches (PICA, AICA, SCA, PCA).
levels.phd:
**Developmental logic.** The brainstem derives from the mesencephalon and the rhombencephalon. The hindbrain is transiently segmented into about eight **rhombomeres**, each with a combinatorial **Hox** code that specifies which branchiomotor nuclei and neural crest streams it produces. Rhombomeres 2–3 give the trigeminal motor neurons; rhombomere 4 gives the facial motor neurons, which then migrate caudally. That migration explains why facial axons loop around the abducens nucleus (the internal genu) before exiting.

**Columns.** In the embryonic neural tube the **sulcus limitans** separates basal (motor) from alar (sensory) plates. When the central canal opens into the fourth ventricle, the alar plate swings laterally, so motor columns end up medial and sensory columns lateral on the ventricular floor. Classically there are seven functional components, arranged roughly medial to lateral: general somatic efferent (III, IV, VI, XII), special visceral or branchial efferent (V motor, VII, nucleus ambiguus), general visceral efferent (Edinger–Westphal, salivatory nuclei, dorsal motor nucleus of X), general and special visceral afferent (both in the solitary nucleus), general somatic afferent (trigeminal sensory complex) and special somatic afferent (vestibular and cochlear nuclei). Newer molecular work suggests the branchiomotor neurons are better seen as a visceral motor class, an argument based on shared transcription factors such as Phox2b.

**Why the brainstem is lethal territory.** Lesion volume and clinical effect scale very differently here than in cortex: a few millimeters can interrupt the corticospinal tract, a cranial nerve nucleus and the ascending arousal system at once. This density is why crossed syndromes (ipsilateral cranial nerve, contralateral body) localize so precisely.

**Comparative note.** Brainstem circuits for breathing, swallowing and eye movement are highly conserved across vertebrates, which has made lamprey and rodent preparations powerful models; extrapolation to humans still requires caution, particularly for arousal networks.
levels.expert:
A neurosurgeon treats the brainstem as the most eloquent tissue in the body. Almost every cubic millimeter contains something that cannot be lost, so surgery here is about corridors, mapping and restraint.

**Approaches.** The brainstem is reached through natural corridors around it rather than through brain: retrosigmoid (cerebellopontine angle, lateral pons), telovelar (through the cerebellomedullary fissure to the floor of the fourth ventricle), suboccipital (dorsal medulla), and subtemporal or pretemporal routes to the ventral midbrain. The choice is driven by where a lesion comes closest to the surface; many surgeons use a "two-point" method, drawing a line from the lesion center through its nearest surface point to pick the approach.

**Safe entry zones.** Published zones are areas where fewer critical structures cross the surface: for example the lateral mesencephalic sulcus, the peritrigeminal zone of the lateral pons, the regions just above and below the facial colliculus, and the olivary zone of the medulla. They are relatively safe, not safe; anatomy distorted by a lesion may not match the textbook map.

**Mapping and monitoring.** Before entering the fourth ventricle floor, surgeons stimulate it to find the facial colliculus and hypoglossal nucleus, which can be displaced. Motor and somatosensory evoked potentials, and free-running EMG of facial and lower cranial nerve muscles, give warnings in real time.

**Typical lesions.** Cavernous malformations (operated mainly after repeated hemorrhage and when they reach a surface), pilocytic astrocytomas, and diffuse midline gliomas in children, which are generally not resectable and are biopsied or treated with radiation.

**Pitfalls.** Postoperative risks include swallowing and airway problems from lower cranial nerve injury, so extubation timing and aspiration precautions are planned in advance. Swelling after surgery can worsen deficits for days before they improve.

keyPoints: The brainstem = midbrain, pons, medulla; it sits in the posterior fossa in front of the cerebellum.
Rule of four: CN III–IV midbrain, V–VIII pons, IX–XII medulla.
CN IV is the only cranial nerve to exit the dorsal brainstem.
Motor nuclei lie medial, sensory nuclei lateral (sulcus limitans).
Each level has tectum (midbrain only), tegmentum and basis.
Blood supply is vertebrobasilar: paramedian, short and long circumferential branches.

examples.src: A small stroke in the left pons causes weakness of the right arm and leg plus a left-sided eye movement problem.
examples.tr: Crossed findings (cranial nerve on one side, body on the other) point to the brainstem.

examples.src: An MRI shows a tumor at the cerebellopontine angle.
examples.tr: That is where CN VII and VIII leave the brainstem, so facial weakness and hearing loss are expected.

examples.src: A surgeon stimulates the floor of the fourth ventricle before cutting into it.
examples.tr: Mapping finds the facial colliculus and hypoglossal nucleus, which a lesion may have pushed out of place.

test.q: Which is the correct top-to-bottom order of the brainstem?
test.explain: The midbrain sits under the thalamus, then the pons, then the medulla, which becomes the spinal cord.

test.q: Which cranial nerve exits from the dorsal surface of the brainstem?
test.explain: Trochlear fibers decussate and exit dorsally below the inferior colliculus. All others exit ventrally or laterally.

test.q: Cranial nerves V to VIII are associated mainly with the:
test.explain: Rule of four: V, VI, VII, VIII belong to the pons (VIII at the pontomedullary junction).

test.q: CN XII exits the medulla between the:
test.explain: The hypoglossal rootlets emerge in the preolivary sulcus. IX, X and XI use the postolivary sulcus.

test.q: The facial colliculus is formed by:
choices: The abducens nucleus and the internal genu of the facial nerve
test.explain: Facial axons loop over the abducens nucleus, raising a bump on the fourth ventricle floor.

test.q: In the brainstem, motor nuclei generally lie:
test.explain: The sulcus limitans separates medial (basal plate, motor) from lateral (alar plate, sensory) columns.

test.q: The tectum (colliculi) is found in the:
test.explain: Only the midbrain has a tectum: two superior and two inferior colliculi.

test.q: Which artery runs in the basilar sulcus on the front of the pons?
test.explain: The two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery, which lies in this groove.

test.q: A patient has a left CN deficit and right-sided body weakness. Where is the lesion most likely?
test.explain: Cranial nerve signs are ipsilateral; the corticospinal tract crosses lower down, so body weakness is contralateral.

test.q: Which cerebellar peduncle connects the cerebellum mainly to the pons?
test.explain: The middle cerebellar peduncle carries pontocerebellar fibers, the largest input to the cerebellum.

test.q: Name the space in the back of the skull that holds the brainstem and cerebellum.
test.explain: The posterior cranial fossa lies below the tentorium cerebelli.

test.q: The medulla becomes the spinal cord at the foramen ___.
test.explain: The foramen magnum is the large hole at the base of the skull.

test.q: The groove that separates motor and sensory columns in the brainstem is the sulcus ___.
test.explain: The sulcus limitans divides the basal (motor) and alar (sensory) plates.

test.q: Which numbered cranial nerve exits at the interpeduncular fossa? (number only, e.g. 3)
test.explain: The oculomotor nerve leaves the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles.

advancedTest.q: Facial motor axons loop around the abducens nucleus because:
choices: Facial motor neurons migrate caudally during development after their axons have started growing
The fourth ventricle pushes them dorsally
The facial nerve is a sensory nerve
The abducens nucleus migrates rostrally through the facial nerve
advancedTest.explain: Facial branchiomotor neurons born in rhombomere 4 migrate caudally, dragging their axons into a loop: the internal genu.

advancedTest.q: Which nucleus is a general somatic efferent (GSE) nucleus?
choices: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
advancedTest.explain: GSE nuclei: III, IV, VI, XII. Ambiguus and facial are branchial; the dorsal motor nucleus of X is visceral efferent.

advancedTest.q: For a brainstem cavernous malformation, the 'two-point' method helps the surgeon:
choices: Choose the approach where the lesion comes closest to the surface
advancedTest.explain: A line from the lesion center through its nearest surface point indicates the best corridor.

advancedTest.q: Why are lower cranial nerve deficits a major postoperative concern after medullary surgery?
choices: They impair swallowing and airway protection, risking aspiration
advancedTest.explain: IX, X and XII control swallowing, the larynx and the tongue; injury risks aspiration, so extubation is planned carefully.

lessons.title: The Midbrain

levels.kid:
The midbrain is the top part of your brainstem. It is small, but it is very busy.

On its back are four little bumps. The top two help your eyes turn quickly toward something that moves, like a ball flying at you. The bottom two help you turn toward a sudden sound, like a door slamming.

Inside the midbrain is a dark strip that makes a helper chemical called dopamine. Dopamine helps you move smoothly. When those cells get sick, people can get shaky.

The midbrain also has a nerve that opens and closes the black dot in your eye, the pupil. Shine a light, and the pupil gets small!
levels.hs:
The **midbrain** (mesencephalon) is the top and shortest part of the brainstem, sitting just under the thalamus. A narrow canal called the **cerebral aqueduct** runs through it, carrying cerebrospinal fluid from the third ventricle to the fourth.

Viewed in cross-section it looks a bit like a face, and it has three layers:

- **Tectum** (roof): four bumps called colliculi. The **superior colliculi** help aim your eyes at things you see. The **inferior colliculi** relay hearing up to the thalamus.
- **Tegmentum** (middle): contains the nuclei for **cranial nerves III and IV** (eye movement and pupil control), the **red nucleus** (movement coordination) and the **periaqueductal gray**, which helps the brain turn down pain.
- **Cerebral peduncles** (front): huge bundles of fibers carrying motor commands from the cortex down to the body. Just behind them is the **substantia nigra**, a dark band of dopamine-making cells. Losing these cells causes **Parkinson's disease**.

The midbrain matters a lot in emergencies. If brain swelling pushes part of the temporal lobe down past a stiff membrane (the tentorium), it can squash the third cranial nerve. That makes one pupil large and unreactive, a "blown pupil," which is a warning sign that doctors check for immediately in head injury.

If the aqueduct gets blocked, fluid builds up above it, causing **hydrocephalus**.
levels.college:
**Superior colliculus level.** Dorsally: superior colliculi (visual orienting, saccade targeting) and, just rostral, the **pretectal area** (pupillary light reflex). Around the aqueduct: **periaqueductal gray** (PAG). In the tegmentum: the **oculomotor nuclear complex** and **Edinger–Westphal nucleus** (preganglionic parasympathetic to the ciliary ganglion), the **red nucleus**, the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract laterally, and the MLF. Ventrally: **substantia nigra** (pars compacta, dopaminergic to the striatum; pars reticulata, GABAergic basal ganglia output) and the **crus cerebri** (frontopontine fibers medially, corticobulbar and corticospinal fibers in the middle, parieto-temporo-occipitopontine fibers laterally). CN III fascicles pass through the red nucleus and exit into the interpeduncular fossa.

**Inferior colliculus level.** Inferior colliculi (auditory relay to the MGN), **trochlear nucleus**, and the **decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles**. Trochlear fibers run dorsally and cross in the superior medullary velum.

**Vertical gaze.** The **rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF** (riMLF) and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal, at the midbrain–diencephalon junction, coordinate vertical saccades and gaze holding.

**Syndromes:**
- **Weber**: ventral midbrain (CN III fascicles plus crus) → ipsilateral CN III palsy, contralateral hemiparesis. Usually PCA perforators.
- **Benedikt**: tegmentum (CN III plus red nucleus) → ipsilateral CN III palsy, contralateral tremor and ataxia.
- **Claude**: CN III plus dorsal red nucleus/cerebellar outflow → ipsilateral CN III palsy, contralateral ataxia.
- **Parinaud (dorsal midbrain)**: upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus and eyelid retraction (Collier sign). Classic causes: pineal tumors and hydrocephalus.

**Herniation.** Uncal herniation compresses CN III (ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil). Compression of the opposite crus against the tentorial edge (**Kernohan notch**) can cause hemiparesis on the same side as the mass, a false localizing sign.
levels.phd:
**Superior colliculus as a priority map.** The intermediate and deep layers of the superior colliculus contain a topographic motor map: activity at one point encodes a saccade vector, and microstimulation evokes fixed-vector saccades. Current models treat it as a **priority map** that integrates visual salience with goals and reward, with a population vector rather than single neurons determining saccade metrics. Collicular lesions in primates cause surprisingly modest long-term saccade deficits because frontal eye fields provide a parallel route, but combined lesions abolish visually guided saccades.

**Dopamine heterogeneity.** The substantia nigra pars compacta and ventral tegmental area (VTA) are no longer seen as uniform reward-prediction-error signalers. Subpopulations differ by projection target, molecular markers and response properties: some respond to salience or aversive events, and some co-release glutamate or GABA. In Parkinson's disease, ventrolateral (tier) nigral neurons projecting to the dorsal putamen degenerate first, while VTA neurons are relatively spared, a pattern linked to high mitochondrial stress from autonomous pacemaking with L-type calcium channels and to large unmyelinated axonal arbors.

**PAG.** The PAG is organized into longitudinal columns that coordinate defensive behaviors: in rodent studies, dorsolateral and lateral columns support active coping (fight or flight, non-opioid analgesia) and the ventrolateral column supports passive coping (freezing, opioid-mediated analgesia). Descending control runs through the rostral ventromedial medulla to the dorsal horn.

**Imaging correlates.** Midbrain atrophy with a relatively preserved pons gives the sagittal "hummingbird" appearance in progressive supranuclear palsy, which also causes vertical gaze palsy; the sign is specific but imperfectly sensitive. Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI and loss of the dorsolateral nigral hyperintensity (the "swallow tail" sign) on susceptibility imaging are being studied as markers of nigral degeneration, though neither replaces clinical diagnosis.
levels.expert:
**The pupil is the first midbrain exam.** In a head-injured or comatose patient, a unilaterally dilated, poorly reactive pupil means CN III compression until proven otherwise, usually from uncal herniation by an expanding hematoma. Parasympathetic fibers ride on the outside of the nerve, so the pupil often changes before eye movements do. Bilateral fixed pupils with loss of other brainstem reflexes suggests central herniation, and secondary midbrain and pontine (Duret) hemorrhages carry a grim prognosis.

**False localization.** A Kernohan notch can produce weakness on the same side as the hematoma. Neurosurgeons operate on the side shown by imaging and, without imaging, the side of the dilated pupil, which is a more reliable guide than the side of weakness.

**Aqueductal stenosis.** Triventricular hydrocephalus (enlarged lateral and third ventricles, normal fourth) is the classic indication for **endoscopic third ventriculostomy**, which creates an opening in the floor of the third ventricle to bypass the aqueduct. The basilar artery tip lies just beneath the floor, so the stoma is placed in front of it, between the mammillary bodies and the infundibular recess.

**Pineal region.** Tumors here compress the dorsal midbrain and the aqueduct, causing Parinaud syndrome and hydrocephalus. Workup includes MRI of the whole neuraxis and tumor markers in serum and CSF, because germinomas may be treated without major resection. Approaches include supracerebellar infratentorial and occipital transtentorial corridors, with the deep veins (internal cerebral veins, vein of Galen, basal veins) as the main hazard.

**Movement disorder surgery.** The subthalamic nucleus, a key DBS target, sits just above the substantia nigra. During microelectrode recording the surgeon listens for the change from subthalamic firing to the more regular high-frequency pattern of the pars reticulata, which signals the electrode has gone deep enough. Stimulation spreading into the oculomotor fascicles can cause eye deviation, which helps define lead position.

keyPoints: The midbrain has tectum (colliculi), tegmentum (CN III, IV nuclei, red nucleus, PAG) and cerebral peduncles.
Superior colliculus = visual orienting; inferior colliculus = auditory relay to the MGN.
Substantia nigra pars compacta makes dopamine; its loss causes Parkinson's disease.
Weber = CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis; Benedikt adds the red nucleus (tremor/ataxia).
Parinaud: upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus, lid retraction.
A blown pupil after head injury = CN III compression from uncal herniation.

examples.src: After a fall, a man becomes drowsy and his right pupil becomes large and sluggish.
examples.tr: Right uncal herniation compressing the right CN III, usually from a hematoma: an emergency.

examples.src: A teenager with headaches cannot look up and his pupils react poorly to light but constrict when he looks at something near.
examples.tr: Parinaud syndrome from a pineal region tumor pressing on the dorsal midbrain.

examples.src: An older woman has a left droopy eyelid with the eye turned down and out, plus right arm and leg weakness.
examples.tr: Weber syndrome: left ventral midbrain lesion hitting CN III fascicles and the left crus cerebri.

lessons.title: The Pons

levels.kid:
The pons is the middle part of your brainstem. It looks like a round bump, almost like a little belly. Pons means "bridge," because it connects the brain to the cerebellum, the part that helps you balance.

The pons holds the switches for several nerves. One lets you chew. One lets you smile and close your eyes. One turns your eyes to the side, like when you look left and right before crossing the street.

The pons also helps you breathe in a smooth rhythm and helps with dreams while you sleep.

Messages from the brain to your arms and legs travel right through the pons on their way down.
levels.hs:
The **pons** is the middle part of the brainstem, the large bulge between the midbrain and medulla. Its name means "bridge," and it really is one: it carries signals from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum on the other side, through thick fiber bundles called the **middle cerebellar peduncles**.

The pons has two main regions:

- **Basilar pons** (front): contains the motor tracts heading to the body and the **pontine nuclei**, which pass cortical plans to the cerebellum.
- **Tegmentum** (back): contains cranial nerve nuclei and pathways.

Four cranial nerves are tied to the pons:

- **CN V (trigeminal)**: face sensation and chewing muscles
- **CN VI (abducens)**: moves the eye outward
- **CN VII (facial)**: facial expression and taste
- **CN VIII (vestibulocochlear)**: hearing and balance, at the junction with the medulla

The pons also contains a center that controls **side-to-side eye movements**, and regions that help regulate breathing, sleep (especially dreaming, REM sleep) and bladder control.

A blockage of the basilar artery can destroy the front of the pons on both sides, causing **locked-in syndrome**: the person is fully awake and aware but cannot move or speak, except for blinking and moving the eyes up and down.
levels.college:
**Basilar pons.** Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers are broken into bundles by the **pontine nuclei**, which receive corticopontine fibers and send crossed transverse fibers into the contralateral middle cerebellar peduncle.

**Caudal pontine tegmentum.** The **abducens nucleus** (with facial genu over it), the **facial motor nucleus** (ventrolateral), the **PPRF** (paramedian pontine reticular formation, horizontal saccade generator), the **MLF**, the vestibular nuclei, the superior olivary complex and trapezoid body (sound localization), the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract, and the medial lemniscus, which is now oriented horizontally.

**Mid pons.** The **principal sensory** and **motor nuclei of CN V**, where the trigeminal root enters laterally.

**Rostral pons.** The **locus coeruleus** (noradrenaline), the parabrachial nuclei, and the superior cerebellar peduncles forming the walls of the upper fourth ventricle.

**Horizontal gaze circuit.** PPRF → ipsilateral abducens nucleus → (1) ipsilateral lateral rectus and (2) internuclear neurons that cross and ascend in the contralateral **MLF** to the medial rectus subnucleus of CN III. Lesions:
- **Abducens nucleus**: ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy (not just a weak lateral rectus).
- **MLF (internuclear ophthalmoplegia, INO)**: the eye on the lesion side fails to adduct on contralateral gaze, the abducting eye shows nystagmus, and convergence is usually preserved. Bilateral INO in a young adult suggests MS.
- **One-and-a-half syndrome**: PPRF or abducens nucleus plus the adjacent MLF; the only horizontal movement left is abduction of the opposite eye.

**Syndromes.** Millard–Gubler (ventral caudal pons): ipsilateral CN VI and VII palsy plus contralateral hemiparesis. Foville (dorsal caudal pons): ipsilateral gaze palsy and facial palsy, ± contralateral hemiparesis. Lateral pontine (AICA): ipsilateral facial palsy, hearing loss, vertigo, ataxia, facial pain/temperature loss and Horner; contralateral body pain/temperature loss. **Locked-in syndrome**: bilateral basis pontis infarction.

**Pontine hemorrhage** (often hypertensive) gives coma, quadriparesis and pinpoint but reactive pupils.
levels.phd:
**Locus coeruleus and adaptive gain.** The locus coeruleus (LC) is a small nucleus that supplies noradrenaline to virtually the whole forebrain, cerebellum and spinal cord. Adaptive gain theory (Aston-Jones and Cohen) proposes two modes: **phasic** bursts locked to task-relevant events, which support focused exploitation, and elevated **tonic** firing with weaker phasic responses, which supports disengagement and exploration. Pupil diameter tracks LC activity closely enough to be used as a rough noninvasive index, though other nuclei also influence the pupil. Newer tracing work shows the LC is more modular than once thought, with partly separate ensembles projecting to different targets.

**LC and neurodegeneration.** In postmortem series, abnormal tau appears in the LC very early, in some cases decades before cortical involvement, which has led Braak and others to propose the LC as an early site in Alzheimer pathology. Whether tau spreads from there or the LC is simply selectively vulnerable remains debated.

**Saccade generation.** Horizontal saccades arise from **excitatory burst neurons** in the PPRF, which are held silent by **omnipause neurons** in the nucleus raphe interpositus. Omnipause neurons stop firing during each saccade, releasing the burst. Burst neurons encode velocity; a neural integrator in the nucleus prepositus hypoglossi and medial vestibular nucleus converts that velocity signal into the steady position signal needed to hold gaze. Failure of the integrator produces gaze-evoked nystagmus.

**REM sleep circuitry.** Glutamatergic neurons of the sublaterodorsal nucleus in the dorsal pons are thought to generate REM atonia via medullary and spinal inhibitory interneurons. Damage to this pathway is linked to **REM sleep behavior disorder**, in which people act out dreams; this disorder is now recognized as a strong early marker of synuclein disorders such as Parkinson's disease, a finding consistent with Braak's caudal-to-rostral staging of synuclein pathology.
levels.expert:
**Cerebellopontine angle.** The CPA is one of the busiest neurosurgical spaces: vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, epidermoids, and the neurovascular conflicts behind trigeminal neuralgia and hemifacial spasm. The retrosigmoid craniotomy is the workhorse approach. During vestibular schwannoma removal the facial nerve is usually stretched thin over the front of the tumor and cannot be seen at first, so it is found with a stimulator and tracked by continuous facial EMG. Facial function outcomes are graded on the House–Brackmann scale.

**Microvascular decompression.** Classic trigeminal neuralgia is often caused by an artery, most commonly the **superior cerebellar artery**, compressing the trigeminal root near its entry zone into the pons, where central myelin gives way to peripheral myelin. Microvascular decompression moves the vessel away and holds it off with a small Teflon pad. It aims to fix the cause rather than destroy part of the nerve, unlike radiosurgery or percutaneous procedures, which are often chosen for older or higher-risk patients.

**Intrinsic pontine lesions.** In children, a diffusely expanding pontine tumor on MRI is usually a **diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered**. It is not curable by surgery; radiation helps temporarily, and biopsy is now done mainly to obtain molecular information and enter trials. Pontine cavernous malformations that bleed repeatedly and reach a surface can be removed through safe entry zones such as the peritrigeminal zone or the areas above and below the facial colliculus.

**Floor mapping.** Stimulating the fourth ventricle floor before entering locates the facial colliculus. Injury there causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy and facial weakness, a combination that can be devastating.

**Critical care.** Rapid overcorrection of chronic low sodium can cause **osmotic demyelination**, classically in the central pons, sometimes producing a locked-in state days after the correction. In a patient with sudden coma and pinpoint pupils, think pontine hemorrhage or basilar occlusion and get vascular imaging fast, since basilar occlusion may be treatable with thrombectomy.

keyPoints: The basilar pons relays cortex → pontine nuclei → contralateral cerebellum (middle cerebellar peduncle).
CN V, VI, VII and VIII are tied to the pons.
PPRF + abducens nucleus drive horizontal gaze; the MLF links to the opposite medial rectus.
INO = MLF lesion: failed adduction on the lesion side, nystagmus of the abducting eye, convergence spared.
Locked-in syndrome = bilateral ventral pons (basilar occlusion): awake, only vertical eye movements and blinking.
Pontine hemorrhage: coma with pinpoint pupils.

examples.tr: Locked-in syndrome from basilar artery occlusion: needs urgent vascular imaging.

examples.src: A woman has electric-shock pain in her cheek triggered by brushing her teeth; MRI shows an artery touching the trigeminal root.
examples.tr: Classic trigeminal neuralgia; microvascular decompression is one surgical option.

lessons.title: The Medulla

levels.kid:
The medulla is the bottom part of your brainstem. It sits right where your brain turns into your spinal cord, at the base of your skull.

The medulla is like the engine room of a ship. You never think about it, but it keeps the most important machines running. It tells you to breathe in and out. It helps your heart keep a steady beat. It keeps your blood pressure just right.

It also helps you swallow, cough, sneeze and even throw up when something bad is in your tummy.

Messages to your arms and legs cross over here, which is why the left side of your brain moves the right side of your body.
levels.hs:
The **medulla oblongata** is the lowest part of the brainstem. It runs from the pons down to the foramen magnum, where it becomes the spinal cord.

On the front of the medulla are two ridges called **pyramids**, which carry the motor (corticospinal) tract. At the bottom of the medulla most of these fibers cross to the other side, in the **pyramidal decussation**. That is why each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body. Beside each pyramid is an oval bump, the **olive**, which sends signals to the cerebellum.

The medulla holds the nuclei of **cranial nerves IX, X, XI and XII**:

- **IX (glossopharyngeal)** and **X (vagus)**: swallowing, voice, gag reflex, and signals to and from the heart, lungs and gut
- **XI (accessory)**: neck and shoulder muscles
- **XII (hypoglossal)**: the tongue

Most importantly, the medulla contains **vital centers** that control breathing rhythm, heart rate and blood pressure, plus reflexes like coughing, swallowing and vomiting.

Because of this, damage to the medulla can be deadly. If pressure in the skull rises enough to push the bottom of the cerebellum (the tonsils) down into the foramen magnum, the medulla gets squeezed and breathing can stop. Strokes in the medulla can cause trouble swallowing, dizziness and unusual numbness patterns.
levels.college:
**Caudal (closed) medulla.** Contains the central canal, the **pyramidal decussation**, and the **nucleus gracilis and cuneatus**. Their axons arc ventromedially as internal arcuate fibers and cross to form the **medial lemniscus** (sensory decussation). The spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract lie dorsolaterally.

**Rostral (open) medulla.** Forms the lower floor of the fourth ventricle. Medial to lateral on the floor: **hypoglossal nucleus**, **dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus**, **nucleus solitarius** (taste and visceral afferents), and vestibular nuclei. Deeper: **nucleus ambiguus** (branchial motor to pharynx and larynx via IX and X), the **inferior olivary nucleus** (climbing fibers to the cerebellum), the **inferior cerebellar peduncle**, the spinothalamic tract and descending sympathetic fibers laterally. The **area postrema**, a circumventricular organ without a blood–brain barrier, triggers vomiting.

**Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome** (anterior spinal or paramedian vertebral branches):
- Contralateral arm and leg weakness (pyramid)
- Contralateral loss of vibration and position sense (medial lemniscus)
- Ipsilateral tongue weakness; the tongue deviates toward the lesion (XII)

**Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome** (vertebral artery more often than PICA itself):
- Ipsilateral loss of facial pain and temperature (spinal trigeminal); contralateral loss of body pain and temperature (spinothalamic)
- Dysphagia, hoarseness, reduced gag (nucleus ambiguus)
- Vertigo, nystagmus, nausea (vestibular nuclei); ipsilateral limb ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle)
- Ipsilateral Horner syndrome; hiccups
- Strength is spared, because the pyramids are medial

**Vital centers.** Inspiratory rhythm arises in the **preBötzinger complex** of the ventrolateral medulla. The **rostral ventrolateral medulla** maintains sympathetic vasomotor tone; the nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus provide vagal cardiac slowing; the baroreceptor reflex runs through the solitary nucleus.

**Tonsillar herniation** compresses the medulla, causing hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing (Cushing's triad) and then respiratory arrest.
levels.phd:
**Generating the breath.** The preBötzinger complex (preBötC), identified in 1991 in neonatal rodent brainstem slices, can keep producing inspiratory rhythm even when isolated in a slice. Rhythm appears to emerge from recurrent excitation among a small population of glutamatergic neurons, with intrinsic bursting currents (persistent sodium and calcium-activated nonselective cation currents) shaping it; the relative roles of network and pacemaker properties are still argued over. A second oscillator, the **parafacial respiratory group**, drives active expiration during exercise or high CO2. Most of these circuits were mapped in rodents, so human detail rests mainly on postmortem anatomy and pathology.

**Opioids and breathing.** PreBötC neurons and the nearby Kölliker–Fuse nucleus in the pons express mu-opioid receptors. Opioid-induced respiratory depression reflects suppression at both sites, which is why opioid overdose slows and then stops breathing while the person may still appear only sedated. This mechanism is a central reason opioid antagonists are lifesaving.

**Chemoreception.** CO2 sensing depends heavily on the **retrotrapezoid nucleus**, a group of Phox2b-expressing neurons near the ventral surface. Mutations in **PHOX2B** cause congenital central hypoventilation syndrome, in which affected children breathe adequately awake but hypoventilate during sleep because automatic CO2-driven breathing is defective. This links a single developmental gene to a specific brainstem function.

**Area postrema.** Lacking a blood–brain barrier, it samples blood for toxins and signals vomiting through the solitary nucleus. It expresses receptors for dopamine, serotonin (5-HT3) and neurokinin-1, explaining why antiemetics target those systems. It is also a target in **neuromyelitis optica**: aquaporin-4 antibodies can cause an "area postrema syndrome" of unexplained hiccups, nausea and vomiting, sometimes as the first sign of the disease.

**Olivocerebellar timing.** Inferior olivary neurons are electrically coupled by gap junctions and oscillate below firing threshold; their climbing fibers are thought to provide timing and error signals for cerebellar learning.
levels.expert:
**Missed medullary strokes.** Lateral medullary syndrome often presents to the emergency department as dizziness and vomiting without arm or leg weakness, so it can be mislabeled as an inner-ear problem. Clues are a hoarse voice, trouble swallowing, a droopy eyelid with a small pupil, and loss of pain sensation on one side of the face and the opposite body. Early MRI can be falsely negative in small posterior circulation strokes, so a careful bedside exam matters. Anyone with suspected medullary stroke stays nil by mouth until a formal swallow assessment, because aspiration pneumonia is a common cause of death.

**Chiari I malformation.** Cerebellar tonsils extend below the foramen magnum (5 mm or more is the usual radiological threshold) and can obstruct CSF flow, causing headaches worse with coughing or straining and sometimes a **syrinx** in the spinal cord. Symptomatic patients may undergo posterior fossa decompression: removing part of the occipital bone and often the rear arch of C1, with or without opening and patching the dura. Imaging findings alone, without matching symptoms, usually do not justify surgery.

**Foramen magnum surgery.** Ventral and ventrolateral lesions, such as foramen magnum meningiomas and vertebral or PICA aneurysms, are reached through the **far-lateral approach**, which removes part of the occipital condyle when needed. The lower cranial nerves and the vertebral artery are the main hazards; IX, X and XI run through the jugular foramen right in the working field, and PICA loops among their rootlets.

**Pressure and the medulla.** Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) means the medulla is being compressed and herniation is imminent. Posterior fossa masses such as cerebellar hemorrhage or infarct with swelling can compress the brainstem quickly; suboccipital decompression can be lifesaving.

**Brain death testing.** The apnea test checks whether rising CO2 triggers any breathing effort. No effort despite an adequate CO2 rise, together with the other criteria, indicates loss of medullary function.

keyPoints: The medulla links pons to spinal cord at the foramen magnum; pyramids carry the corticospinal tract.
Both the motor (pyramidal) and sensory (medial lemniscus) decussations occur in the medulla.
CN IX, X, XI and XII nuclei: nucleus ambiguus, solitary nucleus, dorsal motor nucleus of X, hypoglossal nucleus.
Medial medullary syndrome: contralateral weakness and proprioceptive loss, tongue deviates toward the lesion.
Lateral medullary (Wallenberg): crossed pain/temperature loss, dysphagia, hoarseness, vertigo, ataxia, Horner; strength spared.
Vital centers: preBötzinger complex (breathing), RVLM (vasomotor tone); tonsillar herniation causes respiratory arrest.

lessons.title: Reticular Formation & Vital Centers

levels.kid:
Deep inside your brainstem is a tangle of nerve cells that looks like a fishing net. It is called the reticular formation, which means "little net."

This net is like your brain's alarm clock and light switch. When it sends messages up, your brain wakes up and pays attention. When it quiets down, you fall asleep.

Close by are the "vital centers." Vital means needed for life. These centers keep you breathing, keep your heart beating and keep your blood pressure steady, all by themselves.

If someone gets badly hurt and this net stops working, they can go into a deep sleep called a coma, where they can't wake up.
levels.hs:
The **reticular formation** is a network of neurons running up the core of the entire brainstem, from the medulla to the midbrain. "Reticular" means net-like, because under a microscope its cells and fibers look tangled together rather than grouped into neat nuclei.

It has several big jobs:

- **Wakefulness and attention.** Its upward projections, together with nearby chemical systems, make up the **ascending reticular activating system (ARAS)**. It sends signals through the thalamus to the cortex and keeps the brain awake and alert. Damage to it, or to both cerebral hemispheres, can cause **coma**.
- **Vital functions.** Groups of neurons in the pons and medulla control **breathing**, **heart rate** and **blood pressure**, and run reflexes like swallowing, coughing, sneezing and vomiting.
- **Posture and movement.** Reticulospinal tracts help keep you upright and support walking.
- **Pain control.** Some reticular neurons send signals down the spinal cord to turn down pain.

Chemical "broadcasting" systems also start here. The **raphe nuclei** release serotonin, the **locus coeruleus** releases noradrenaline, and other groups release acetylcholine. They affect mood, sleep and alertness all over the brain.

Doctors test brainstem function in an unconscious patient with simple reflexes: shining a light in the eyes, touching the cornea, and checking the gag and cough reflexes.
levels.college:
**Organization.** Three longitudinal zones: the midline **raphe nuclei** (serotonergic), a **medial magnocellular zone** (large neurons giving rise to the pontine and medullary reticulospinal tracts) and a **lateral parvocellular zone** (local circuits for cranial nerve reflexes and autonomic integration).

**Arousal.** The ARAS, first described physiologically by Moruzzi and Magoun in 1949, is now understood as several parallel systems: cholinergic neurons of the **pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei**, noradrenergic **locus coeruleus**, serotonergic **raphe**, dopaminergic **VTA**, and glutamatergic parabrachial neurons. These project to the **intralaminar thalamic nuclei** and to the hypothalamus and basal forebrain, which in turn activate the cortex. Hypothalamic histamine (tuberomammillary) and orexin (lateral hypothalamus) neurons complete the network.

**Coma localization.** Coma requires either bilateral cortical or diffuse dysfunction, or a lesion of the arousal system, most critically in the rostral pontine and midbrain tegmentum. A unilateral hemispheric lesion causes coma only when it compresses the brainstem or the opposite side.

**Vital centers:**
- **Respiration**: dorsal respiratory group (nucleus solitarius), ventral respiratory group (including the preBötzinger complex), and pontine respiratory group (parabrachial and Kölliker–Fuse, which smooths the switch from inspiration to expiration).
- **Cardiovascular**: the **RVLM** drives sympathetic tone; baroreceptor input reaches the solitary nucleus, which excites the caudal ventrolateral medulla, which inhibits the RVLM.
- Pattern generators for swallowing, coughing and vomiting; the **pontine micturition center**.

**Brainstem reflexes in coma:**
- Pupillary light (II → III)
- Corneal (V → VII)
- Oculocephalic and cold caloric (VIII → III, VI via MLF)
- Gag (IX → X) and cough (X)

**Posturing.** Decorticate (arm flexion, leg extension) suggests damage above the red nucleus; decerebrate (arm and leg extension) suggests damage at or below the midbrain and carries a worse prognosis.
levels.phd:
**From "reticular" to networks.** The old picture of a diffuse, undifferentiated net has been replaced by a set of chemically defined nuclei with specific projections. Human connectivity studies, combining diffusion imaging with histology, have mapped an **ascending arousal network** linking brainstem nuclei to the thalamus, hypothalamus and basal forebrain, then to cortical hubs such as the default mode network. Lesion mapping in patients with brainstem coma has highlighted a small region of the rostral pontine tegmentum, near the parabrachial and pedunculopontine nuclei, as especially critical. Rodent work suggests glutamatergic parabrachial neurons are particularly important, possibly more than the classic cholinergic systems; how well that maps onto humans is still being tested.

**The sleep–wake switch.** Saper and colleagues proposed a "flip-flop" model: GABAergic sleep-promoting neurons of the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus and the arousal nuclei inhibit each other, which makes transitions rapid and states stable. Orexin neurons stabilize the switch in the wake position. Loss of orexin neurons, probably autoimmune, causes **narcolepsy type 1**, with unstable states and intrusions of REM features such as cataplexy into wakefulness.

**Anesthesia and arousal.** General anesthetics act at many molecular targets, but converging evidence suggests they produce unconsciousness partly by suppressing arousal nuclei and thalamocortical communication. In rodents, stimulating dopaminergic or cholinergic arousal pathways during anesthesia can speed emergence, suggesting emergence is an active process rather than passive washout.

**Disorders of consciousness.** Patients can be in coma, a vegetative state (now often called unresponsive wakefulness syndrome) with sleep–wake cycles but no awareness, or a minimally conscious state with inconsistent signs of awareness. Functional MRI studies have shown that a minority of behaviorally unresponsive patients can follow commands mentally ("cognitive motor dissociation"), challenging bedside diagnosis and raising major ethical questions. Central thalamic deep brain stimulation has been tried experimentally in a small number of patients.
levels.expert:
**The coma exam is a localization exercise.** Start with airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, and the cause you can treat fast. Then answer one question: is this a structural lesion of the brainstem or hemispheres, or a diffuse metabolic or toxic process? Metabolic coma usually spares the pupillary light reflex until late, which helps separate it from structural coma. Opioid toxicity, with small pupils and slow breathing, is a classic mimic of pontine injury.

**What to document.** Glasgow Coma Scale (eye, verbal, motor), or the FOUR score, which adds brainstem reflexes and breathing pattern and is useful in intubated patients. Record pupils (size, symmetry, reactivity), corneals, oculocephalic or caloric responses, gag, cough, motor response to central pain, and breathing pattern. Trends matter more than a single number: a falling motor score or new pupil asymmetry triggers a repeat CT.

**Breathing patterns.** Cheyne–Stokes respiration suggests bilateral hemispheric or diencephalic dysfunction (and is common in heart failure); central neurogenic hyperventilation is classically linked to midbrain or upper pontine lesions; apneustic breathing to the pons; ataxic breathing to the medulla, which often comes right before apnea. These localizations come from classic case series and are imperfect, so they support rather than replace imaging.

**Neurosurgical decisions.** Extensor posturing or loss of brainstem reflexes after trauma with a surgical mass lesion usually means urgent evacuation. Prognosis should never rest on one early exam, especially with sedation, hypothermia, or drugs on board. Many centers wait at least 72 hours after cardiac arrest before prognosticating and combine several tests.

**Brain death.** Determination requires a known, irreversible cause, exclusion of confounders (sedatives, hypothermia, severe metabolic derangement), absent brainstem reflexes, no response to pain within the head, and a positive apnea test. Ancillary tests such as cerebral blood flow studies are used when the clinical exam cannot be completed.

keyPoints: The reticular formation is a network through the brainstem core: raphe (midline), medial magnocellular and lateral parvocellular zones.
The ascending arousal system (ARAS) projects via thalamus, hypothalamus and basal forebrain to keep the cortex awake.
Coma = bilateral hemispheric dysfunction or a lesion of the rostral pons/midbrain tegmentum.
Vital centers in pons and medulla control breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing and vomiting.
Brainstem reflexes: pupillary (II–III), corneal (V–VII), oculocephalic/caloric (VIII–III/VI), gag (IX–X).
Decorticate posturing = above the red nucleus; decerebrate = midbrain or below (worse).

examples.tr: Opioid toxicity can mimic pontine injury; check for a reversible cause first.

examples.tr: Decerebrate (extensor) posturing: injury at or below the midbrain, a sign of severe damage.

examples.src: A comatose patient's eyes stay fixed in the head when it is turned side to side.

test.q: The ascending reticular activating system mainly controls:
test.explain: It keeps the cortex awake through thalamic and other relays.

test.q: The raphe nuclei release:
test.explain: The midline raphe column is serotonergic.

test.q: A small lesion causing coma is most likely in the:
test.explain: This is where the arousal pathways are concentrated.

test.q: The corneal reflex tests which nerves?
test.explain: Touching the cornea (V) makes the eyelids blink (VII).

test.q: The gag reflex tests which nerves?
test.explain: IX carries the sensation; X drives the pharyngeal muscles.

test.q: Which posture suggests the deeper (worse) brainstem injury?
test.explain: Decerebrate posturing indicates damage at or below the midbrain.

test.q: Which neurons drive sympathetic tone to blood vessels?
test.explain: The RVLM keeps blood pressure up; the baroreflex inhibits it.

test.q: Loss of orexin neurons causes:
test.explain: Orexin stabilizes wakefulness.

test.q: Ataxic (irregular) breathing in coma is classically linked to the:
test.explain: It often precedes apnea.

test.q: What 3-part bedside scale scores eyes, verbal and motor responses? (abbreviation)
test.explain: Scores range from 3 to 15.

test.q: The brainstem reflex tested by shining light in the eye uses CN II and CN ___.
test.explain: Optic in, oculomotor (parasympathetic) out.

test.q: In the apnea test, doctors check whether rising ___ triggers breathing.
test.explain: No breathing effort despite adequate CO2 rise indicates loss of medullary function.

test.q: Name the pontine center that controls bladder emptying (3 words).
test.explain: Also called Barrington's nucleus.

kidTest.q: The reticular formation looks like a:
kidTest.explain: Reticular means little net.

kidTest.q: When the net sends messages up, you:
kidTest.explain: It is the brain's alarm clock.

kidTest.q: 'Vital' means:
kidTest.explain: Vital centers keep you alive.

kidTest.q: The vital centers keep you:
kidTest.explain: Breathing, heartbeat and blood pressure.

kidTest.q: A deep sleep where someone can't wake up is called a ___.
kidTest.explain: It can happen if the brainstem net stops working.

kidTest.q: Do the vital centers need you to think about them?
kidTest.explain: They are automatic.

advancedTest.q: Which pupil finding best separates metabolic from structural coma?
choices: Preserved light reflex suggests metabolic coma
Bilateral fixed dilated pupils suggest metabolic coma
advancedTest.explain: Metabolic coma typically spares the pupillary light reflex until late.

advancedTest.q: In Saper's flip-flop model, what makes sleep–wake transitions fast and states stable?
choices: Gap junctions in the inferior olive
Mutual inhibition between VLPO and arousal nuclei, stabilized by orexin
advancedTest.explain: Mutual inhibition creates bistability; orexin biases toward wake.

advancedTest.q: 'Cognitive motor dissociation' refers to:
choices: Behaviorally unresponsive patients who show command-following on fMRI or EEG
Recovery of motor function before speech
Patients who move but cannot think
advancedTest.explain: It shows bedside exams can miss covert awareness.

advancedTest.q: Why do many guidelines wait at least 72 hours after cardiac arrest before prognosticating?
choices: Sedation, hypothermia and evolving injury make early exams unreliable
Brain death is impossible before 72 hours
advancedTest.explain: Premature prognosis risks self-fulfilling withdrawal of care.
